notes: r10-02 replaces event-specific-handler-logic with separate-independent-effects to avoid repeating r10-04. r11-10 replaces compiler-not-every-function with compiler-memoization-not-shared. r11-11 combines the planned useMemo and useCallback escape-hatch facts; r11-12 tests whether useCallback invokes its function. r12-06 replaces useoptimistic-update-function with the React 19 useActionState rename.

cards.statement: An Effect can synchronize a browser API with component state after rendering.
cards.explanation: Effects synchronize components with external systems, including browser APIs. React runs their setup after rendering.

cards.statement: A component's event handler runs again whenever that component re-renders.
cards.explanation: An event handler runs when its associated interaction occurs. Re-rendering the component does not invoke the handler.
cards.misconception: Rendering a component invokes its event handlers.

cards.statement: React runs an Effect's setup while calculating the component's JSX.
cards.explanation: React runs Effect setup after the component commits. Calculating JSX happens during rendering.
cards.misconception: Effect setup is part of rendering.

cards.statement: React runs an Effect's previous cleanup before setup with changed dependencies.
cards.explanation: When dependencies change, React cleans up synchronization using the old values before setting it up with the new values.

cards.statement: React runs a provided Effect cleanup when the component unmounts.
cards.explanation: A cleanup function returned from Effect setup stops or undoes its synchronization when the component leaves the page.

cards.statement: An Effect can omit a prop read by its setup from the dependency array when that prop changes rarely.
cards.explanation: An Effect's dependency array includes reactive values its setup reads, including props. How often a prop changes does not remove that dependency.
cards.misconception: Rarely changing props may be omitted from Effect dependencies.

cards.statement: An Effect with [] dependencies re-runs whenever its component updates state.
cards.explanation: An empty dependency array keeps state and prop updates from re-synchronizing that Effect.
cards.misconception: An empty dependency array behaves like an omitted dependency array.

cards.statement: React generally runs Effects after paint for updates outside user interactions.
cards.explanation: For an update unrelated to an interaction, React generally lets the browser paint the updated screen before running the Effect.

cards.statement: React defers click-caused Effects until after the browser paints.
cards.explanation: When an interaction such as a click causes an Effect, React may run it before the browser paints. Paint timing is not fixed for these Effects.
cards.misconception: Interaction-caused Effects run after paint in every case.

cards.statement: Server rendering runs useEffect setup after generating HTML.
cards.explanation: Effects run on the client. Server rendering does not execute useEffect setup.
cards.misconception: Server rendering runs Effects after producing HTML.

cards.statement: useLayoutEffect runs before the browser paints the updated screen.
cards.explanation: useLayoutEffect runs after the DOM commit and before repaint, making it suitable for layout measurements that affect the visible result.

cards.statement: Since React 19.2, useEffectEvent reads current props without resynchronizing its Effect.
cards.explanation: An Effect Event sees the latest committed props and state while its surrounding Effect remains reactive only to its own dependencies.

cards.statement: An Effect that copies a derived value into state can save a render pass.
cards.explanation: Copying a calculated value into state from an Effect adds a render with the stale value, then another with the updated value. Calculate it during rendering.
cards.misconception: An Effect makes derived display state cheaper to update.

source.title: You Might Not Need an Effect

cards.statement: React's documentation recommends separate Effects for unrelated synchronization processes.
cards.explanation: Separate Effects let each synchronization process react to its own dependencies. A change to one process need not restart another.

cards.statement: A chain of state-setting Effects reduces the number of render passes.
cards.explanation: When Effects update state to trigger further Effects, each step can cause another render pass.
cards.misconception: Chaining state updates through Effects avoids intermediate renders.

source.title: You Might Not Need an Effect

cards.statement: React's documentation recommends notifying a parent of a toggle through an Effect.
cards.explanation: For a toggle caused by an interaction, call the parent's callback during the same event that updates the child.
cards.misconception: An Effect is the preferred place to report an interaction to a parent.

source.title: You Might Not Need an Effect

cards.statement: useSyncExternalStore subscribes a component to data held outside React.
cards.explanation: useSyncExternalStore reads an external store's snapshot and subscribes to changes so React can update the component.

cards.statement: getSnapshot may return a fresh object on repeated calls while its store stays unchanged.
cards.explanation: While the store is unchanged, getSnapshot must return the same value. A mutable store needs a cached immutable snapshot.
cards.misconception: A newly allocated but equivalent snapshot is safe on each read.

cards.statement: An Effect fetching data can use cleanup to prevent a stale response from updating state.
cards.explanation: The cleanup can mark an earlier request as obsolete; its response handler then ignores the result instead of overwriting newer data.

source.title: You Might Not Need an Effect

cards.statement: Recreating an options object on re-renders keeps an Effect's dependency stable.
cards.explanation: A newly created options object has a new identity. If the Effect depends on that object, it can re-synchronize after each commit.
cards.misconception: Equal object fields make an object dependency stable.

cards.statement: Declaring a helper function inside an Effect removes it from the Effect's dependency list.
cards.explanation: A function declared inside the Effect is part of its setup rather than a reactive value created during component rendering.

cards.statement: Custom Hooks package stateful logic for reuse across components.
cards.explanation: A custom Hook extracts recurring stateful behavior behind a reusable function that components call.

cards.statement: Two components calling the same custom Hook can share the Hook's local useState state.
cards.explanation: Each call to a custom Hook has independent local state. Reusing the Hook's code does not merge its callers' useState values.
cards.misconception: Calling the same custom Hook shares one local state cell.

cards.statement: A custom Hook can call useState and useEffect inside its body.
cards.explanation: Custom Hooks compose built-in Hooks, so their top-level code can call useState and useEffect.

cards.statement: useMemo usually returns its cached calculation result while dependencies remain equal.
cards.explanation: useMemo stores a calculation result for reuse on later renders when its listed dependencies have not changed.

cards.statement: useMemo keeps a cached value when an object dependency has equal contents but a new identity.
cards.explanation: useMemo compares dependencies with Object.is. A newly created object differs from the prior object even when their fields match.
cards.misconception: useMemo compares object dependencies by their contents.

cards.statement: useCallback usually returns the previous function while dependencies remain equal.
cards.explanation: useCallback caches a function value between renders until its dependencies change.

cards.statement: memo compares the whole props object by reference before skipping a render.
cards.explanation: By default, memo compares each prop with Object.is. The props object itself is not the unit of comparison.
cards.misconception: memo requires the entire props object to retain one identity.

cards.statement: memo guarantees a stable-props child skips its render function.
cards.explanation: memo usually skips a parent-driven re-render when props stay equal, but React may still render the component. It is a performance optimization.
cards.misconception: memo provides a semantic guarantee that rendering is skipped.

cards.statement: memo accepts an arePropsEqual function to compare a component's old and new props.
cards.explanation: An optional arePropsEqual function tells memo whether the previous and next props produce the same output and behavior.

cards.statement: React Compiler applies its memoization when a component runs in the browser.
cards.explanation: React Compiler optimizes application code at build time. The browser executes the resulting code.
cards.misconception: React Compiler performs its analysis during browser rendering.

cards.statement: React Compiler can memoize component work across parent re-renders.
cards.explanation: React Compiler analyzes components and inserts memoization that can avoid repeating work when their inputs stay unchanged.

cards.statement: React Compiler can memoize calculations inside compiled custom Hooks.
cards.explanation: React Compiler applies memoization within React Hooks as well as components, including calculations they perform during rendering.

cards.statement: React Compiler shares one memoized calculation across separate components.
cards.explanation: React Compiler's memoization is local to a component or Hook. It does not share one cached result across separate components.
cards.misconception: Compiler-generated caches are shared across component boundaries.

cards.statement: React Compiler accepts useMemo and useCallback as escape hatches for precise memoization.
cards.explanation: With React Compiler enabled, useMemo and useCallback still provide explicit control over which values are memoized.

cards.statement: useCallback invokes the supplied function during the render that declares it.
cards.explanation: useCallback returns the function value; it does not call that function. The caller decides when to invoke it.
cards.misconception: useCallback executes its argument while rendering.

cards.statement: useTransition marks updates inside startTransition as non-blocking Transitions.
cards.explanation: State updates marked as Transitions run in the background so urgent interactions remain responsive.

cards.statement: In React 19, useTransition sets isPending after its async Action resolves.
cards.explanation: useTransition sets isPending when the Transition starts and keeps it true until its Actions complete and the final state appears.
cards.misconception: An async Action becomes pending only after its Promise resolves.

cards.statement: In React 19, useActionState returns state, an Action dispatcher, and a pending flag.
cards.explanation: useActionState returns the current state, a dispatchAction function, and an isPending value for its dispatched Actions.

cards.statement: In React 19, a useActionState Action receives FormData as its first argument.
cards.explanation: The Action passed to useActionState receives previous state first. When used for a form, submitted FormData follows it.
cards.misconception: A useActionState form Action receives FormData before previous state.

cards.statement: In React 19, useOptimistic shows a temporary value while an Action is pending.
cards.explanation: useOptimistic displays an optimistic state during a pending Action, then returns to the supplied base value when the Action ends.

cards.statement: In React 19, useFormState is the current name of the Action state Hook.
cards.explanation: The React 19 Hook is useActionState. It was called ReactDOM.useFormState in Canary releases; useFormState was renamed and deprecated.
cards.misconception: The Canary name useFormState remains the current React 19 API.

cards.statement: In React 19, a function passed to a form's action prop receives submitted FormData.
cards.explanation: A function used as a form action handles the submission in a Transition and receives the submitted form data.

cards.statement: In React 19, a submit button's formAction function runs alongside the form's action function.
cards.explanation: A submit button's formAction overrides the enclosing form's action for that submission.
cards.misconception: formAction adds a second Action to the form submission.

cards.statement: In React 19, a successful form Action automatically resets the form's uncontrolled fields.
cards.explanation: After a function form action succeeds, React resets uncontrolled field elements in that form.

cards.statement: In React 19, useFormStatus reports submission status for the form returned by its own component.
cards.explanation: useFormStatus from react-dom reads a parent form's status. Calling it in a component that renders the form does not track that form.
cards.misconception: useFormStatus tracks a form created in the same component.

cards.statement: In React 19, use(promise) shows a Suspense fallback while the Promise is pending.
cards.explanation: Reading a pending Promise with use suspends the component. A surrounding Suspense boundary shows its fallback until resolution.

cards.statement: In React 19, use(promise) may send a rejected Promise to the nearest Suspense fallback.
cards.explanation: A rejected Promise read with use displays the nearest Error Boundary's fallback. Suspense handles the pending state.
cards.misconception: Suspense handles Promise rejection as a loading fallback.
